newsitem.title: USA: Swiss avoid major problem with humanitarian fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss avoid major problem with humanitarian fund.

text.p: Switzerland's U.S. critics praised its decision on Wednesday to set up a huge humanitarian fund with some saying the move both restores a shattered image and blunts an expected harsh Clinton administration report on Swiss-Nazi dealings.

New York Republican Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, who has been waging a one-man war with the Swiss over its Second World War role, said the decision to establish the $4.7 billion fund from Swiss gold reserves was "a breakthrough declaration."

He added, "It is the first significant ackowledgment from individuals in responsible positions in Switzerland that massive wrongdoing occurred. It will take massive resources to begin the process of healing. President (Armold) Koller is to be commended. It is long overdue."

Edgar Bronfman, the president of the World Jewish Congress who pressed the Swiss for months to make such a gesture, said, "We hail President Koller's announcement as representing a victory for the Swiss and Jewish peoples."

Abraham Foxman, the head of the Anti-Defamation League, a Jewish civil rights group, said the Swiss move now puts pressure on the other nations neutral during the war, Sweden, Spain, Turkey and Portugal, to come to terms with their wartime roles.

Koller proposed a "Swiss Foundation for Solidarity" to aid victims of poverty, human rights abuses, genocide, the Holocaust and natural disasters in Berne's boldest response yet to charges that it coldly profited the war by acting as money launderers for Hitler's Third Reich.

If adopted, the fund could draw on around seven billion Swiss francs ($4.7 billion) in funds from official gold reserves -- meaning that since it would not be using taxpayers money, it would not be subject to a referendum under Swizterland's form of direct democracy.

One U.S. source close to the Swiss decision said the timing of the announcement was interesting because it comes about three or four weeks before the Clinton Administration is to make public a scathing report on Swiss dealings with the Nazis.

Many think the report will be so scathing that it will force the United States to consider reopening a 1946 treaty in which the Swiss agreed to return $58 million in gold it bought from the Nazis. According to those familiar with the report, it will confirm that Switzerland bought or stored more than $400 million in gold from the Germans during the war.

"The report, which is still being complied and draws on documents that have been secret for over 50 years, is going to say that after the war Switzerland returned only about 15 percent of the looted gold it bought from the Nazis," one source said.
Once that report is out, Switzerland will face enormous pressure, the source said, adding that the fund decision will help mitigate an expected onslaught of bad publicity.
"But the fund is not being established for negative reasons. It also helps to restore the Swiss reputation for postive neutrality, something the Swiss people are very proud of," the source said.
